Application shell

The application shell is what every page shares: the navigation, a header, and the places where dialogs and toasts appear. Shadleaf has two layouts for it, both built from the Sidebar family:

  • The sidebar layout (shadcn/ui’s sidebar-07): the navigation in a column beside the page. It collapses to a strip of icons on a desktop.
  • The header layout (after Flux’s header-inset): the navigation as a row of links in a site header across the top.

In both, the navigation is one <sl:sidebar>. Below 768 px the menu button opens that same element as a panel over the page, so the two layouts work the same way on a phone. Copy one of them into your application (the samples keep theirs in templates/layout/main.html) and change what you need: the templates are yours, and so is the CSS around the components.

Which one

Section titled “Which one”
Sidebar layout Header layout
Pages in the navigation Many, in labelled groups, with sub-menus A handful of top-level pages
On a desktop A column the user collapses to icons (or out of view) and the cookie remembers A row of links that scrolls sideways when it does not fit; never collapses
Page header Inside the page: trigger, breadcrumb, theme toggle The site header itself: name, links, theme toggle
Room for the page The width minus the sidebar (3 rem collapsed to icons) The full width
On a phone The panel The same panel
Sample sample-01 sample-02 (strict Content-Security-Policy)

Pick the sidebar layout when the application has more pages than fit in a header row or needs groups and sub-menus. Pick the header layout for a smaller application. Moving from one to the other later means changing the layout template, not the pages: both take the same pageTitle and content.

What every layout needs

Section titled “What every layout needs”

Whichever you choose, the layout template has the same pieces. The two layouts below have all of them:

  • In the head, ~{sl/layout :: theme-script} and then ~{sl/layout :: assets}, then your own stylesheet. The theme script sets the dark class before the first paint. Under a strict policy it needs its nonce or hash (see Content-Security-Policy).
  • <sl:skip-link/> first in the body. It lets a keyboard user jump past the navigation to the page.
  • One main: <sl:sidebar-inset> renders <main id="main" tabindex="-1">, the skip link’s target. Put nothing of the page outside it.
  • The page’s title in the <title> and as the page’s h1, from the same pageTitle parameter.
  • The current page marked in the navigation with th:active="${#slNav.current('/people')}", which reads the request, so no controller has to say which page it is.
  • <sl:toaster> at the end of the body, with the toasts a controller put in the toasts flash attribute before a redirect (see Toast).
  • A <div id="modal-root">, if htmx fetches dialogs into the page (see Dialog).

The CSS for the page itself (its padding, the h1, the logo in the sidebar) is the application’s. Shadleaf’s CSS styles its components, not the page around them.

The sidebar layout

Section titled “The sidebar layout”

shadcn/ui’s sidebar-07 block with the inset variant, as the layout of the first sample application (sample-01’s layout/main.html, which has four groups): the application’s name and logo at the top, groups of pages (one of them collapsible), a footer, and the page as a card beside it with a site header holding the trigger, a separator, the page’s breadcrumb and the theme toggle. The sidebar collapses to icons, with a tooltip on every menu button. hx-boost on the body loads every page with htmx (see With htmx).

A page passes its title, its breadcrumb’s levels and its content. The levels are a th:block with th:ref, so nothing of it is rendered where it stands; the layout puts them in its <sl:breadcrumb-list>:

The header’s layout is the site header’s own: a row 3.5 rem high, the trigger, a short separator and the breadcrumb at the start, the end slot at the end. The page’s padding and the logo are the application’s. Without Tailwind:

The Sidebar page has every part and option: the variants, collapsing off-canvas instead of to icons, the sidebar at the end of the line, badges and actions.

The header layout

Section titled “The header layout”

For an application with a handful of pages: the layout of the second sample application (sample-02’s layout/main.html, which runs under a strict Content-Security-Policy), after Flux’s header-inset layout. The header holds the menu button (on a phone), the application’s name, the pages as a row of links, and the theme toggle and the user menu at the end; More (Settings, Help) and the panel’s own header are panel-only. The page is a card below the header (variant="inset"). Sample-02 also has an Admin link for admins only, left out here: see Navigation by role.

On a phone the menu button opens the same navigation as a panel, with the icons, the group labels and the panel-only parts:

The page in the card is the application’s again; sample-02 keeps it to a readable width:

.app-logo is the sidebar layout’s. In the row, the links show their labels without icons and the current page is marked as in the sidebar; group actions, separators and collapsible items are left out of the row, and the trigger is hidden on a desktop. See In the header and Panel-only parts.

A page without the navigation

Section titled “A page without the navigation”

A sign-in page has nothing to navigate to yet. Sample-02 gives it a layout of its own: the site header with only the name and the theme toggle, and the page in a plain main with the skip link’s target:

Without <sl:sidebar-provider> the site header lies across the top of the page, on the page’s colour with a border below.

With htmx

Section titled “With htmx”

hx-boost on the body (as the sidebar layout has it) loads every page with htmx. The server renders the whole page each time, so the current page, the breadcrumb and the sidebar’s collapsed state are always right, and a link in the phone panel closes it. The Sidebar page says what happens with history and when only the main area is boosted.

A boosted link sends HX-Request too. A controller that answers other htmx requests with a fragment (a table’s rows, a dialog) has to tell such a request apart, or a link in the navigation gets the fragment without the page around it. A request from the body’s boost has HX-Boosted and no HX-Target, because the body has no id. With htmx-spring-boot:

A link inside an element with an hx-target of its own (a table’s sort and page links, boosted to swap only the table) does send HX-Target, and still gets its fragment. See Tables with htmx.

A boosted link or form made after the session expired would get the sign-in page swapped into the body (or, for a form, nothing at all, as its CSRF token went with the session). The Spring Security guide shows how to send the browser to the page instead, which then asks the user to sign in and comes back to it: htmx after the session expired.

A sidebar below a full-width header

Section titled “A sidebar below a full-width header”

shadcn/ui’s sidebar-16 puts a header across the whole top of the page and the sidebar below it. Shadleaf does not support that layout. From 768 px the sidebar is sticky at the top of the screen and as tall as the screen, so below a header it would slide under the header and run past the bottom of the screen. <sl:sidebar-provider> has to start at the top of the page. Put the page’s header inside <sl:sidebar-inset> (the sidebar layout), or put the navigation in the header (the header layout).

The signed-in user

Section titled “The signed-in user”

Both layouts have a place for the user: the sidebar’s footer, and the site header’s end slot. The user menu goes in either (as="header" in the site header): the signed-in user from Spring Security with a menu that signs out, or a Sign in link for an anonymous visitor, so one layout serves public pages too. Sign out posts a form with the CSRF token; hx-boost="false" on it keeps a boosted body from sending it with htmx. Where the user comes from, and how to change it, is in the Spring Security guide.

Navigation by role

Section titled “Navigation by role”

Some pages are only for some users. Hide their links with the Thymeleaf extras for Spring Security, which Spring Boot configures when the dependency is there (also with Spring Security 7, under its springsecurity6 name):

Declare the sec namespace on the layout’s <html> (xmlns:sec="http://www.thymeleaf.org/extras/spring-security") and put sec:authorize on the menu item, so no empty list item is left behind:

There is one navigation, so the phone panel follows the same rule as the sidebar or the header row. A group whose items are all for one role takes the attribute on the <sl:sidebar-group> instead, label included.

Hiding a link is no security. Anyone can type the address. What keeps other users out is the rule on the URL:

A user without the role who opens /admin gets a 403. The same attribute works on content inside a page: a button only admins may use, a column only they may see. Sample-02 has both: an Admin page in its header row, and a Manage access button on its Data page, shown to Ada (an admin) and not to Grace. With sec:authorize-url="/admin" instead, the template asks whether the URL rule lets the user in, so link and rule cannot disagree.

Test both sides with spring-security-test: the link is in the page for one user and not for another, and the URL answers 403 without the role.

The Spring Security guide has the same in short, next to where the signed-in user comes from.
